{"id": "2:16/q23", "question": "How is مهتدين parsed and formed?", "turns_on": "Predicate of كان versus circumstantial analysis.", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q23/p1", "position": "It is the accusative predicate of كان, from plural مهتديين.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Ṭabrisī give the syntax. {"id": "2:16/q24", "question": "What occasion or setting is reported for this passage?", "turns_on": "General hypocrites, foretelling, or Ibn Ubayy.", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q24/p1", "position": "It concerns hypocrites generally.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports the exegetes; Ibn ʿĀshūr reads 2:8 onward collectively."}, {"id": "2:16/q24/p2", "position": "It foretells a people before they existed.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports unseen disclosure."}, {"id": "2:16/q24/p3", "position": "The meeting verse concerns ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and companions.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports his praise of Abū Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿAlī to believers, followed by his claim to have turned them away; the earlier passage remains general."}]}
{"id": "2:16/q25", "question": "How does this verse connect with the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q25/p1", "position": "It sums up the hypocrites' portrait, explains wandering, and contrasts their end with the guided.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī relates it to 2:15; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the detached sentence restates that ending and contrasts 2:5 and 2:7. {"id": "2:16/q26", "question": "What broader lesson does the trade image teach?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q26/p1", "position": "Life is a trade whose true gain requires guidance and upright conduct.", "reasons": "Sufyān al-Thawrī asks everyone to examine their trade, citing 61:10. {"id": "2:16/q28", "question": "Is metaphor possible in the Qur'an, as this attribution illustrates?", "turns_on": "Whether divine speech can use metaphor.", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q28/p1", "position": "Yes: rational metaphor attributes an action to a related cause.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī reports the majority, distinguishes resemblance from association, and cites Pharaoh, Satan, recited verses and other causes. {"id": "2:16/q29", "question": "How is the nearby pronoun hāʾ pronounced?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q29/p1", "position": "Ibn Kathīr lengthens its vowel with a matching glide.", "reasons": "Ibn Khalawayh reports yāʾ after kasra and wāw after ḍamma; other readers indicate the vowel without an extra letter to avoid adjacent consonants around weak hāʾ."}]}
{"id": "2:16/q30", "question": "How is the nearby مستهزئون pronounced?", "turns_on": "Full hamza versus lightening or replacement.", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q30/p1", "position": "The hamza is articulated fully, with a lighter intermediate form also possible.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj prefers full articulation; the lightened hamza lies between wāw and hamza."}, {"id": "2:16/q30/p2", "position": "Its hamza may become yāʾ, while dropping it outright is weak.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj gives مستهزيون and calls مستهزون weak except under a dialectal hamza-to-yāʾ change."}]}
{"id": "2:16/q31", "question": "What do nearby يمدهم and طغيانهم mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q31/p1", "position": "They mean giving respite and their excess or unbelief.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj supplies the two glosses for the neighboring passage."}]}
{"id": "2:16/q32", "question": "What does nearby يعمهون mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q32/p1", "position": "They wander in confusion, blind to guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj cites عمه and عامه for a confused person and an anonymous rajaz poet for confused people blind to guidance."}]}
{"id": "2:175/q01", "question": "Who are those indicated by 'those'?", "turns_on": "Whether the description is tied to the preceding scripture concealors or applied to hypocrites.", "positions": [{"id": "2:175/q01/p1", "position": "The people who concealed scripture, specifically Jewish scholars or Jews who knew Muhammad's description.", "reasons": "Muqatil and al-Tabari identify prior belief or knowledge of Muhammad; al-Tabari specifies scholars concealing his prophethood for bribes. Al-Mawardi calls them the previously mentioned Jewish scholars; Abu Hayyan and Ata in al-Durr link them to the preceding concealors and 2:174."}, {"id": "2:175/q01/p2", "position": "The hypocrites whose conduct shows readiness to enter the Fire.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya transmits Qatada, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Rabi describing the subjects as hypocrites."}]}
{"id": "2:175/q02", "question": "What does their purchase of error and punishment mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:175/q02/p1", "position": "They chose error over available guidance and thereby chose punishment over the forgiveness that following guidance would have brought.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Wahidi, al-Tabrisi, al-Razi, al-Nasafi, and Ibn Kathir specify denial or concealment of Muhammad's scriptural description despite knowledge; al-Baydawi and al-Alusi add worldly profit. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi explain the second exchange as the consequence of the first. Abu Hayyan says buying implies desire and extreme loss; Bint al-Shati notes that bāʾ marks what is surrendered, citing 9:9. Damghani compares purchase in 9:111, where believers sell themselves to God. Al-Biqai says concealment misled others and added their burden; al-Tabatabai says the deed takes embodied form as eating fire and the persistent deed is concealment. Al-Razi contrasts knowledge with ignorance in this world and forgiveness with punishment in the next. Bursawi says the price is metaphorical, and Elmalili calls the acquired error and torment lasting. Al-Jishumi states explicitly that no actual sale occurred. His reported alternative specifies forsaking repentance, the path to forgiveness, in favor of obstinacy."}, {"id": "2:175/q02/p2", "position": "Error and guidance here also stand for their outcomes: punishment and reward or Paradise; the exchange is Hell for Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi reports this identification of misguidance with punishment and guidance with reward and Paradise."}]}
{"id": "2:175/q03", "question": "Why is the exchange of punishment for forgiveness stated after the exchange of error for guidance?", "turns_on": "Whether the second exchange restates the first exchange's result or adds a separate charge of knowing disobedience.", "positions": [{"id": "2:175/q03/p1", "position": "It reinforces the preceding exchange by naming its consequence.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim calls it reinforcement. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi explain that punishment follows chosen error and forgiveness would follow discarded guidance. Al-Jishumi attributes this confirmation reading to al-Aṣamm and Abū Muslim."}, {"id": "2:175/q03/p2", "position": "It adds a distinct charge: they knowingly persisted in disobedience and chose punishment over forgiveness.", "reasons": "Al-Qadi's explanation is preferred by al-Tabrisi for adding a distinct meaning; al-Razi stresses their prior knowledge of reward and punishment. Al-Jishumi prefers al-Qāḍī's explanation for its additional benefit. Al-Qāḍī distinguishes ignorance from knowing the consequences and still choosing the causes of Hell. Al-Jishumi also reports a distinct reading in which they forsook repentance that brings forgiveness and persisted in obstinacy."}]}
{"id": "2:175/q04", "question": "How does the purchase sentence and its following fāʾ connect to the preceding threat?", "turns_on": "The sentence's syntactic relation to the earlier condemnation.", "positions": [{"id": "2:175/q04/p1", "position": "The fāʾ makes their astonishing relation to the Fire follow from their exchange of guidance and forgiveness.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi says it answers the preceding description of their trade."}, {"id": "2:175/q04/p2", "position": "The purchase sentence explains the severe threat as an independent answer or as a second predicate about the ugliness of concealment.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi gives both syntactic connections: the first predicate describes the threat's severity and the second describes concealment's ugliness."}]}

"reasons": "Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Rabi, and others connect boldness to deeds that bring Hell near; several explicitly deny real patience. Al-Farra, al-Kisai, al-Asmai, and others cite a judge's or Bedouin's rebuke mā aṣbaraka ʿalā Allāh for daring against God; al-Thalabi and al-Qurtubi identify Yemeni usage. Al-Tabari prefers this sense from Arabic usage and explains Fire as punishment. Sahl applies it to issuing religious judgments without knowledge of Sunna or law. Al-Qurtubi says conduct leading to Hell is called courage. Al-Biqai likens it to defying a ruler's prison threat. Al-Tabatabai says al-Sadiq's three transmitted explanations converge. Al-Jishumi reports al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and Mujāhid on knowingly facing the Fire; al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and al-Rabīʿ locate this boldness in worldly deeds that lead to it."}, {"id": "2:175/q05/p2", "position": "It describes their persistence in deeds leading to the Fire, despite knowing their consequence.", "reasons": "Al-Muarrij says opposition to the Prophet is known to lead there; al-Kisai and Qutrub supply an understood 'deeds of the Fire's people.' Al-Sadiq speaks of doing what they know leads to it. Bursawi takes Fire as its cause and describes the persistence as the object of human wonder. The Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya reports distinguish this from physical endurance. Al-Jishumi transmits al-Kisāʾī and Quṭrub's alternative sense of persisting in the Fire's deeds. Abū al-Fatḥ supplies 'the deeds of the people of the Fire' as the understood complement."}, {"id": "2:175/q05/p3", "position": "It is a rebuking question: what made them endure the Fire or pursue its causes after trading truth for falsehood?", "reasons": "Al-Majaz and Abu Ubayda take mā as 'what'; Ata, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, and others call it a question. Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash argues from case endings. Al-Mubarrad cites a prohibition on tormenting a living creature and a poem for the sense 'make endure,' but Ibn Atiyya disputes his vocalization; Abu Hayyan argues the causative hamza cannot simply mean ṣabara. Al-Zajjaj uses the analogy of enduring hunger. Some phrase it as asking what drove them to the deeds; al-Qurtubi calls it belittling dismissal, and Kur'an Yolu a forceful warning. An alternative reported by Ibn Jinnī asks what led them to endure the consequences that warrant the Fire. Al-Jishumi attributes the rebuking question to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd, and al-Suddī; another report from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ, and Ibn Zayd asks what emboldened them after abandoning truth for falsehood."}, {"id": "2:175/q05/p4", "position": "It marvels at how long the condemned endure or remain in the Fire itself.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi compare Qur'anic exclamations in 80:17 and 19:38. Ibn Kathir mentions torment and shackles. Ibn Ashur treats certain future suffering as already witnessed, comparing Zuhayr, Malik ibn al-Rayb, and 102:5–6. Abu Hayyan reports a figurative sense of remaining in the Fire. Al-Jishumi reports al-Kisāʾī and Quṭrub's sense 'how long they remain in the Fire' and their comparison with an exclamation about resemblance to Ḥātim's generosity."}, {"id": "2:175/q05/p5", "position": "It asks what keeps them confined in the Fire, or how long God keeps them there.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi takes ṣabara as confining; al-Tabrisi reports Ibn Abbas asking what keeps them confined. Al-Zajjaj compares asking how long someone bears imprisonment; al-Mubarrad cites a poem and a report about confining a living animal, though Ibn Atiyya challenges his vowel analysis. Al-Jishumi transmits al-Farrāʾ's reading of God making them endure or remain in the Fire and al-Zajjāj's analogy of keeping someone in prison."}, {"id": "2:175/q05/p6", "position": "It marvels at how practiced or knowledgeable they are in the deeds of Hell's people or in falsehood.", "reasons": "Mujahid's reported expressions vary between ability, expertise, and knowledge; Ibn Qutayba calls the reading good and supplies an omitted 'deeds.' Al-Thalabi calls it sarcasm. Al-Tabari includes expertise within his preferred exclamation. Al-Jishumi reports Mujāhid's gloss 'how active they are in the deeds of the people of the Fire,' as if restraining themselves for those deeds."}, {"id": "2:175/q05/p7", "position": "Their heedless pursuit of Hell's causes is described sarcastically as if they accept its consequence.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says knowingly choosing Hell's cause makes them seem willing to endure its result in this life. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, and al-Alusi stress lack of concern. Elmalili contrasts unwillingness to give up worldly pleasure with persistence toward eternal burning; Abu Hayyan likens it to defying a ruler."}, {"id": "2:175/q05/p8", "position": "It says how little they are distressed or grieve over the Fire.", "reasons": "Both al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan report this figurative gloss."}, {"id": "2:175/q05/p9", "position": "It describes their actual future patience when silenced in Hell and deprived of escape.", "reasons": "Al-Asamm places the patience after the command to remain there, compared by al-Razi with 23:108. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan reject the temporal shift from present wording and observe that the damned may cry out. Al-Jishumi reports al-Aṣamm locating this patience in the afterlife, when they despair of escape."}, {"id": "2:175/q05/p10", "position": "It negates endurance: God has not made them patient over the Fire.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa and another report take mā as negative; al-Samin dismisses it."}, {"id": "2:175/q05/p11", "position": "It simply makes their state an object of astonishment.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash compares 80:17; al-Tabrisi also cites it and an Arab saying about God's punishment. Abu Hayyan reports that most place the patience in worldly life, whether literal or metaphorical."}]}
{"id": "2:175/q06", "question": "How is mā in 'فما أصبرهم' parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether mā is an exclamatory noun, a question, a relative or described noun requiring an unspoken predicate, or negation.", "positions": [{"id": "2:175/q06/p1", "position": "It is an exclamatory complete indefinite noun in the nominative, subject of a following clause.", "reasons": "Sibawayh and the majority supply 'something made Zayd beautiful' as a model; al-Wahidi calls it a subject and the following past-tense verb its predicate. He says mā's ambiguity creates surprise where shayʾ would diminish it or state a settled fact. Al-Baydawi cites poetry; al-Razi compares the other Arabic exclamation pattern in 19:38. Al-Tabari and Abu Hayyan cite 80:17, and Abu Hayyan adds 54:31. Ibn al-Jawzī says exclamatory mā has an implied sense of 'what' or 'how.' Al-Burhān counts this among three Qurʾanic exclamation forms, with 80:17 and a reading of 82:6 that adds a hamza."}, {"id": "2:175/q06/p2", "position": "It is interrogative with exclamatory force or rhetorical denial.", "reasons": "Al-Farra and Ibn Durustawayh make the next clause its predicate; al-Samin compares 2:28. Al-Razi reports al-Farra's model as denying that anything surpasses Zayd in beauty, with case endings distinguishing this from asking which part of Zayd is best. Al-Jishumi also reports interrogative mā intended as rebuke and reproach."}, {"id": "2:175/q06/p3", "position": "It is a relative pronoun with an omitted predicate.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda and al-Majaz use 'what made them endure'; al-Akhfash analyzes the following clause as its relative. Al-Razi objects that the parallel relative sentence 'the one who made Zayd good' is malformed while the exclamation is complete."}, {"id": "2:175/q06/p4", "position": "It is an indefinite noun described by the following clause, with its predicate omitted.", "reasons": "This is al-Akhfash's second reported analysis, repeated by al-Samin and al-Alusi."}, {"id": "2:175/q06/p5", "position": "It is negative: God has not made them patient with the Fire.", "reasons": "Reported by Abu Hayyan and attributed by al-Samin to Abu al-Baqa, who dismisses it."}]}
{"id": "2:175/q07", "question": "Is the exclamatory aṣbara a verb or a noun, and how does its complement work?", "turns_on": "Whether the fixed exclamative pattern has verbal inflection and a direct object or nominal behavior and an object-like complement.", "positions": [{"id": "2:175/q07/p1", "position": "It is a past-tense verb, with the following accusative as its direct object.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi says its form moved from triliteral to quadriliteral, its fixed final fatḥa marks a verb, and the object is genuinely acted upon; the poetic diminutive mā aḥaysana merely imitates a noun. Basrans cite agreement, fatḥa, and attached accusative pronoun. Al-Samin prefers this parsing; Abu Hayyan states its effect on the object."}, {"id": "2:175/q07/p2", "position": "It is a noun or comparative form, with the following accusative an object-like complement.", "reasons": "Kufans cite noun-like diminutives; al-Razi says an underlying verb would change a middle wāw to alif, allow an intervening adverb, and not be restricted to bare triliteral roots. He rejects the Basran subject paraphrase: it loses wonder, is uninformative, treats mā as an unsuitable indefinite subject, and would make the maker God require 'who,' not 'what.' Attached accusatives also occur with laʿalla and layta; aṣbara can be a comparative noun. Abu Hayyan records the resulting change in the complement's status."}]}

 ṣabr as restraining oneself from what one dislikes. Al-Jishumi reports Mujāhid's application of restraint to sustained activity in the Fire's deeds."}, {"id": "2:175/q08/p2", "position": "Ṣabara can mean to confine or restrain someone, as with a tied animal used as a target.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi notes the prohibited shooting of a bound animal called maṣbūra; al-Mubarrad cites that prohibition and a poem for confinement, but Ibn Atiyya challenges the poem's vowels, reading aṣbarahā as a past form of ṣabara."}, {"id": "2:175/q08/p3", "position": "Aṣbara can mean to command patience or make someone patient, through the causative hamza.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya allows both senses for an interrogative reading; Abu Hayyan insists it means 'make patient' and rejects al-Mubarrad's unsupported equation with simple ṣabara. Al-Tabrisi cites al-Hutay'a's poem for subjecting someone to something disliked. Al-Jishumi reports al-Farrāʾ interpreting the form as God making them endure the Fire."}]}
{"id": "2:175/q09", "question": "How can an exclamation or wonder be attributed to God?", "turns_on": "Whether the exclamation is assigned to human observers or its divine sense is restricted to magnification.", "positions": [{"id": "2:175/q09/p1", "position": "It directs human hearers to marvel or tells them the state merits wonder; God does not experience ignorance or astonishment.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi, Ibn al-Anbari as reported by Ibn al-Jawzi, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, and Bursawi give this account. Al-Tabrisi adds rebuke and reproach; Shurayh rejected a reading of 'I wonder' in 37:12 on the same ground. Abū ʿAlī's argument, transmitted by Ibn ʿAṣfūr in al-Burhān, says astonishment entails ignorance and therefore redirects the expression to the human audience. Al-Jishumi says it can portray conduct that merits wonder. Al-Burhān's learned authorities extend the audience-centered account to divine prayer and hope; Sībawayh interprets 20:44 through Moses and Aaron's own hope, which Ibn al-Dāʿī praises."}, {"id": "2:175/q09/p2", "position": "Divine wonder means magnification alone, whereas human wonder may include ignorance of its cause.", "reasons": "Al-Razi separates the two elements of ordinary wonder; al-Nakha'i compares divine laughter, mockery, and cunning, which likewise do not bear human meanings."}, {"id": "2:175/q09/p3", "position": "Divine astonishment may be affirmed when mā is exclamatory.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports this view and its citation of a reading of 'bal ʿajibtu' with ḍamma."}]}
{"id": "2:175/q10", "question": "What does 'the Fire' stand for in this phrase?", "turns_on": "Whether Fire names punishment and its worldly causes figuratively or evokes the future Fire directly.", "positions": [{"id": "2:175/q10/p1", "position": "It stands for its punishment or for deeds and causes leading to it.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says Fire replaces 'its punishment' and compares ellipsis in praise of Hatim and Antara; al-Samin says 'deeds of Hell' is understood. Bursawi calls Fire the cause by metonymy; al-Tabrisi and al-Kisai/Qutrub understand the deeds of Hell's people. Abū al-Fatḥ, as reported in al-Burhān, supplies 'the deeds of the people of the Fire' after the expression; al-Kisāʾī and Quṭrub also allow persistence in its deeds, according to al-Jishumi."}, {"id": "2:175/q10/p2", "position": "It is the actual future Fire, presented as if already visible.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says certain future torment is imagined as present, comparing Zuhayr and Malik ibn al-Rayb's poetry and 102:5–6."}]}
{"id": "2:175/q11", "question": "What ethical or theological lessons are drawn from their choice?", "turns_on": "The notes draw distinct moral, theological, and embodied-deed consequences from the same choice.", "positions": [{"id": "2:175/q11/p1", "position": "Their unbelief is their own act, and culpable deeds merit punishment; knowing sin is graver.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi cites the verse against the Jabriyya, says curse and punishment follow the actor's actions, and says knowledge increases guilt and punishment."}, {"id": "2:175/q11/p2", "position": "Scholars are warned against hiding truth for gain, status, favors, office, luxury, or leadership.", "reasons": "Bursawi says greed, envy, and desire are an inner fire that devours good deeds; al-Alusi says the worldly motive explains the severe warning."}, {"id": "2:175/q11/p3", "position": "Concealment and its worldly price become embodied as fire and punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabai says deeds take embodied form: choosing a small price becomes eating fire, then exchanging guidance and forgiveness for error and punishment."}]}
{"id": "2:175/q12", "question": "How does the verse connect with the following account of the Book and division?", "turns_on": "Whether the connection explains the punishment, identifies the disputants, or extends the warning to disputes over the Qur'an.", "positions": [{"id": "2:175/q12/p1", "position": "The next verse explains the condemnation: God revealed the true Book, and those who differed over it are in deep division.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi cites 2:176; Bursawi says rejection or concealment of true scripture warrants torment. Abu Hayyan traces the sequence from disbelievers' deafness and blindness through lawful food and necessity to this condemnation, which intensifies from their choice to their opposition to the Book."}, {"id": "2:175/q12/p2", "position": "The people divided over scripture are Jews and Christians, in deep enmity.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi identifies the parties and characterizes their schism."}, {"id": "2:175/q12/p3", "position": "The distant schism warns against disputing the Qur'an and God's signs.", "reasons": "Abu al-Aliya cites 40:4, where only unbelievers dispute God's signs."}]}
{"id": "2:175/q13", "question": "What rhetorical figures are associated with this verse or its imagery?", "turns_on": "The notes name different rhetorical devices or illustrative imagery.", "positions": [{"id": "2:175/q13/p1", "position": "It exemplifies mumāthala or tamthīl, an allusive metaphor whose chosen words exemplify the intended meaning.", "reasons": "Al-Baqillani says Qudama calls it tamthil and sets it against irdaf."}, {"id": "2:175/q13/p2", "position": "Hell's speech, sight, and rage are vivid personifying images like poetry about a corner kissing a footprint and a minbar walking.", "reasons": "Al-Baqillani cites 50:30, 25:12, and 67:8 for the Hell images."}, {"id": "2:175/q13/p3", "position": "Muṭābaqa means mentioning a thing with its opposite, such as night and day or black and white.", "reasons": "Al-Baqillani attributes the common definition to al-Khalil, al-Asmai, and Ibn al-Mutazz."}]}
{"id": "2:175/q14", "question": "What do the nearby descriptions of God's treatment and painful punishment mean?", "turns_on": "The notes discuss different adjacent expressions rather than one disputed reading.", "positions": [{"id": "2:175/q14/p1", "position": "God's not speaking to them marks His anger.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj compares a person refusing to speak to someone through anger."}, {"id": "2:175/q14/p2", "position": "God sends no angels to greet them, or does not let them hear His speech as the righteous do.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj reports these two alternatives in the preceding verse's description."}, {"id": "2:175/q14/p3", "position": "God's not purifying them means He does not praise them, so they are punished.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj glosses wa-lā yuzakkīhim."}, {"id": "2:175/q14/p4", "position": "Alīm means painful or aching, describing intense pain.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj distinguishes muʾlim as intensified pain. Bint al-Shati cites poetry about pain and sleeplessness and notes painful punishment in sixty-eight Qur'anic verses, including 2:10 and 9:61."}, {"id": "2:175/q14/p5", "position": "Kindling a beacon means displaying the light of truth to its seeker.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati reports Ibn al-Athir's gloss of Ali's phrase."}]}
{"id": "2:175/q15", "question": "What orthographic principles are illustrated by nearby Qur'anic spellings?", "turns_on": "The notes give distinct general and symbolic explanations for varying alif spellings.", "positions": [{"id": "2:175/q15/p1", "position": "Mushaf copies differ in spelling some names; omitted letters can motivate retaining another alif.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan lists Harut, Marut, Haman, and Qarun; Dawud retains alif after omission of waw, and most copies likewise retain alif in Isra'il after deleting ya."}, {"id": "2:175/q15/p2", "position": "Sound masculine and feminine plurals generally omit alif, except when followed by hamza or a doubled letter.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan states the orthographic rule."}, {"id": "2:175/q15/p3", "position": "Retaining alif may reflect a lower, visible worldly aspect, while omitting it reflects a higher spiritual aspect.", "reasons": "Abu al-Abbas supplies the principle, comparing 38:75 and 114:4. Al-Burhan applies it to al-firash and al-ta'am, the People of the Book's and believers' food in 5:5, the higher food of 5:75, and intensified shutting of spiritual doors in 12:23 versus concrete doors in 12:25; some contrasts are subtler than others."}]}

{"id": "2:175/q17", "question": "May God be described as al-Ṣabūr in connection with aṣbarahum?", "turns_on": "Whether restraint from something disliked can be predicated of God literally, or al-Ṣabūr can be used figuratively for forbearance.", "positions": [{"id": "2:175/q17/p1", "position": "No; ṣabr denotes restraining oneself from what one dislikes, so al-Ṣabūr is not a divine attribute.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī defines ṣabr this way and denies the divine attribution, as reported by al-Jishumi."}, {"id": "2:175/q17/p2", "position": "Yes, figuratively, in the sense of the Forbearing.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi reports this allowance from other authorities."}]}

{"id": "2:250/q03", "question": "How does the lām in li-Jālūt work?", "turns_on": "Whether the prepositional phrase depends on the stated verb or an omitted circumstantial expression.", "positions": [{"id": "2:250/q03/p1", "position": "It attaches directly to barazū, expressing their advance toward Jalut.", "reasons": "Al-Samin reports this as one possible analysis."}, {"id": "2:250/q03/p2", "position": "It belongs to an implied circumstantial phrase: they advanced intending to meet Jalut.", "reasons": "Al-Samin reports an omitted sense of intended encounter."}]}
{"id": "2:250/q04", "question": "Who was Jalut?", "turns_on": "The sources identify his people differently: Amalekites, Canaanites, or Philistines.", "positions": [{"id": "2:250/q04/p1", "position": "He was the king and commander of the Amalekites.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi give this identification. {"id": "2:250/q05", "question": "How large was Jalut's army?", "turns_on": "Two transmitted counts give different numbers of troops.", "positions": [{"id": "2:250/q05/p1", "position": "It numbered three hundred thousand horsemen.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya cites a report; al-Qurtubi reports the same number and contrasts ʿIkrima's smaller figure."}, {"id": "2:250/q05/p2", "position": "It numbered ninety thousand.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi transmits this figure from ʿIkrima in contrast to the three hundred thousand report."}]}

{"id": "2:250/q07", "question": "What does 'pour patience upon us' convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:250/q07/p1", "position": "It asks God to grant patience in a full, abundant outpouring, as though emptying a vessel over them.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, al-Zajjaj, al-Wahidi, al-Jishumi, al-Tabrisi and al-Razi explain the vessel image and the root's sense of emptiness; al-Jishumi cites 28:10. {"id": "2:250/q08", "question": "What patience did the fighters seek?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:250/q08/p1", "position": "They sought self-restraint and endurance in battle, especially restraint from fleeing.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi defines sabr as restraining the self from what attracts it and says the fighters sought endurance in jihad. {"id": "2:250/q09", "question": "What does making their feet firm mean?", "turns_on": "Whether firm feet chiefly pictures inner resilience or also refers to the ground underfoot.", "positions": [{"id": "2:250/q09/p1", "position": "It means steadfast hearts, courage and resolve so they hold their ground and do not flee.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim reports Ibn Ishaq's gloss.
